teacher_understanding.answer: Gravity and other loads tend to change body position. Appropriate muscle tension supports body segments and stabilises joints.

teacher_understanding.question: How can muscles maintain posture without an obvious movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: They can develop tension while their overall length changes little, balancing the forces that would otherwise move the body.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this function differ from producing body movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Movement changes the position of body parts; posture maintenance helps preserve a position. Both depend on controlled muscle force.

p005-i30.exam_note: Remember posture as a skeletal muscle function in addition to movement.

p005-i31.content: Other names: Skeleton muscle, Striated muscle and voluntary muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Which other names does the book give skeletal muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lists 'Skeleton muscle', 'Striated muscle' and 'voluntary muscle'.

teacher_understanding.question: Which earlier features on this page explain the names associated with skeleton and striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Attachment to bones explains the skeletal association, while alternating dark and light bands explain the name striated muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is skeletal muscle called voluntary muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its activity can generally be initiated and controlled consciously, as when deliberately moving a limb.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the name voluntary mean every skeletal muscle contraction requires conscious choice?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Skeletal muscles also participate in reflexes and automatic postural adjustments. 'Voluntary' describes their capacity for conscious control.

p005-i31.exam_note: Names and their reasons are useful for matching questions; the book prints 'Skeleton muscle'.

p005-i32.where_on_page: Lower right, bordered skeletal muscle illustration
p005-i32.content: Two-part skeletal muscle illustration. On the left, several orange-red elongated cylindrical fibres have repeated transverse bands and multiple blue oval nuclei. On the right, an arm drawing shows red muscle alongside the upper-arm and forearm bones, with the elbow bent. The caption beneath the fibre drawing reads 'Skeletal Muscle'. There are no directional arrows or process stages.
p005-i32.type_note: The image proposal is a placeholder; the illustration teaches skeletal muscle appearance and its association with bones.

teacher_understanding.question: What two views does the skeletal muscle illustration combine?
teacher_understanding.answer: A schematic view of muscle fibres and an anatomical example of an arm muscle associated with bones.

teacher_understanding.question: Which written skeletal muscle characteristics are represented visually?
teacher_understanding.answer: Elongated cylindrical unbranched fibres, banding, multiple nuclei and association with the skeleton.

teacher_understanding.question: How does combining these views improve understanding?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibre view helps identify the tissue's cellular appearance, while the arm view connects that tissue to a familiar body location and movement role.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the blue ovals and orange-red fibres be read as schematic features?
teacher_understanding.answer: The colours make nuclei and fibres easy to distinguish. They are illustrative conventions rather than evidence that living nuclei or fibres have those exact colours.

p005-i32.exam_note: Use the combined appearance, nuclei and attachment features for tissue identification.

p005-i33.where_on_page: Lower-right illustration, below the fibre drawing
p005-i33.content: Skeletal Muscle — identifies the illustrated group of cylindrical, banded muscle fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: What tissue does the label name?
teacher_understanding.answer: Skeletal muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the illustration is directly identified by the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The group of elongated cylindrical fibres shown to the left of the arm drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the identification be supported beyond reading the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The drawing combines unbranched cylindrical fibres, repeated transverse bands and several nuclei, matching the skeletal muscle features listed in the text.

p005-i33.exam_note: Practise identifying the tissue from its features as well as its caption.

p006-i1.content: b. Visceral Muscle/ Smooth muscle tissue
p006-i1.exam_note: Names the muscle type described in the following items.

p006-i2.where_on_page: upper left, below smooth muscle heading

p006-i3.where_on_page: upper left, first smooth muscle bullet
p006-i3.content: • Fibres are spindle shaped/fusiform i.e. pointed at ends/tapering ends.

teacher_understanding.question: What does spindle shaped or fusiform mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibre tapers towards pointed ends. 'Spindle shaped' and 'fusiform' describe the same shape here.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this shape found in the muscle types on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes the fibres of visceral or smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How would a student recognise a fusiform fibre in a drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Look for a wider middle that narrows towards both ends, rather than a fibre of approximately uniform width.

prerequisites: muscle fibre as a muscle cell
p006-i3.exam_note: Spindle shaped or fusiform fibres are a key smooth muscle identifier.

p006-i4.where_on_page: upper left, second smooth muscle bullet
p006-i4.content: • Single and centrally located nucleus in each cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the number of nuclei stated for a smooth muscle cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each cell has a single nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the nucleus located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies centrally within the cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How should nucleus number and nucleus position be recorded separately?
teacher_understanding.answer: Number answers how many nuclei a cell contains; position answers where the nucleus lies. For smooth muscle here, the two observations are one nucleus and a central position.

prerequisites: muscle fibre as a muscle cell
p006-i4.exam_note: Both nucleus number and central location can appear in tissue identification questions.

p006-i5.where_on_page: upper left, third smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What feature is absent from smooth muscle fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: They lack striations, which is consistent with the page's alternative name 'Unstriated'.

teacher_understanding.question: Where would striations be looked for?
teacher_understanding.answer: They would be looked for as repeated bands across the muscle fibre under a microscope.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can smooth muscle contract despite lacking visible striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains contractile proteins, but these are not arranged in the regular repeating sarcomeres that produce the banded appearance of striated muscle.

p006-i5.exam_note: Absence of striations distinguishes smooth muscle from cardiac muscle.

p006-i6.where_on_page: upper left, fourth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page state about branching in smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle fibres are unbranched.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the branching description apply?
teacher_understanding.answer: It applies to the shape of an individual fibre, rather than to the overall outline of an organ containing the tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this help distinguish smooth muscle from cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle fibres are unbranched, whereas the cardiac fibres described below are branched.

p006-i6.exam_note: Branching is a direct comparison criterion for smooth and cardiac muscle.

p006-i7.where_on_page: upper left, fifth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What fatigue characteristic does the book assign to smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The book states that smooth muscle fibres do not fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: What on this page supports teaching this as a smooth muscle characteristic?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is explicitly listed under smooth muscle characteristics. The page provides no experimental evidence or measurements.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this simplified statement be understood physiologically?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle is well suited to sustained activity and can maintain tension with relatively low energy use. The statement expresses fatigue resistance under normal conditions, rather than unlimited performance under any condition.

prerequisites: fatigue as reduced ability to sustain activity
p006-i7.exam_note: A shared stated feature of smooth and cardiac muscle; avoid using fatigue resistance alone to distinguish them.

p006-i8.where_on_page: upper left, sixth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: Which function of smooth muscle is named here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page names peristalsis as a function performed by smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How does peristalsis move material?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated waves of contraction and relaxation in the wall of a hollow organ move its contents along. In the digestive tract, contraction behind a portion of food and relaxation ahead help propel it forward.

teacher_understanding.question: When is digestive peristalsis used?
teacher_understanding.answer: It operates as digestive contents are moved through the tract, without requiring a conscious decision for each movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the contractions be coordinated?
teacher_understanding.answer: A travelling pattern can propel contents along the tube; an isolated squeeze mainly changes the local shape or pressure.

prerequisites: digestive tract as a hollow tube
food movement through the digestive tract
p006-i8.exam_note: Peristalsis is a standard function-to-muscle matching fact.

p006-i9.where_on_page: left, below the smooth muscle bullets

teacher_understanding.question: Which other names are given for smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page gives 'Unstriated' and 'Involuntary muscles'. Its heading also calls it visceral muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the difference between the criteria expressed by unstriated and involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Unstriated describes the absence of visible bands; involuntary describes activity that is not ordinarily under conscious control.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should these names not be treated as interchangeable classification criteria?
teacher_understanding.answer: Appearance and control are different properties. The page itself shows that cardiac muscle is striated while also being involuntary.

p006-i9.exam_note: Tests often distinguish the appearance criterion from the control criterion.

p006-i10.where_on_page: left, last line of the smooth muscle section
p006-i10.content: Example: Stomach, Intestine, eye, blood vessel etc.

teacher_understanding.question: What do the listed examples illustrate?
teacher_understanding.answer: They illustrate structures in which smooth muscle occurs.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page place smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The named examples are the stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessel.

teacher_understanding.question: Where within these examples is the smooth muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in muscular parts of the stomach and intestinal walls, in the walls of many blood vessels, and in structures of the eye such as the iris and ciliary muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How can one tissue type serve these different structures?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its contraction has different effects according to its arrangement: it can move digestive contents, change vessel diameter, or alter pupil size and lens accommodation in the eye.

prerequisites: tissue as a component of an organ
p006-i10.exam_note: Preserve all four named examples for location matching and odd-one-out questions.

p006-i11.where_on_page: upper right, rectangular smooth muscle illustration
p006-i11.content: A boxed illustration pairs a group of elongated orange, spindle shaped cells on the left with a digestive tract illustration on the right. The cells have tapered ends and blue oval nuclei, with no repeated transverse bands drawn. The digestive illustration shows the coiled intestine within the outline of the large intestine. The tissue and organ are placed side by side to associate smooth muscle with the digestive tract; there are no connecting arrows.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the upper figure show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows a schematic of smooth muscle cells beside an intestinal illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visual features agree with the smooth muscle description?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells have tapered ends, blue nuclei within them and no drawn striations.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the side-by-side arrangement be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: It links the tissue to a digestive location where it occurs. It does not show a sequence of events or the detailed mechanism of peristalsis.

p006-i11.exam_note: Supports visual identification and matching a tissue to an organ.

p006-i12.where_on_page: upper right figure, below the orange cell group
p006-i12.content: Smooth Muscle — the label names the group of spindle shaped cells shown above it.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the printed tissue label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The printed label is 'Smooth Muscle'.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the figure does the label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the orange spindle shaped cell group above the words.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the label be checked against the drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: The tapered cells and absence of drawn striations agree with the adjacent smooth muscle characteristics.

p006-i12.exam_note: Provides the tissue name for the visual identification.

p006-i13.exam_note: Names the next muscle tissue type.

p006-i14.where_on_page: middle left, below cardiac muscle heading

p006-i15.where_on_page: middle left, first cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What shape does the page assign to cardiac muscle fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes them as cylindrical.

teacher_understanding.question: Where do these fibres occur according to the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: They occur in the wall of the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cylindrical shape and branching both describe cardiac fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cylindrical describes the elongated body of a fibre, while branching describes extensions from it. A fibre can therefore be cylindrical in its main portions and also branch.

p006-i15.exam_note: Read cylindrical together with branching and striations for identification.

p006-i16.where_on_page: middle left, second cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does uninucleate mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means having one nucleus; the page describes each cardiac fibre this way.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does this nucleus description apply?
teacher_understanding.answer: It applies to the individual cardiac muscle fibre, rather than the heart as a whole.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a teacher qualify the book's statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle cells commonly have one centrally placed nucleus, but some have two. The page presents the usual school-level description.

p006-i16.exam_note: Capture the book's uninucleate description and keep the biological qualification distinct.

p006-i17.where_on_page: middle left, third cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What branching feature is stated for cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle fibres are branched.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this branched muscle tissue located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is located in the heart wall.

teacher_understanding.question: How does branching contribute to the organisation of cardiac tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Branched cells connect with neighbouring cells to form a network. Specialised junctions between cells help transmit force and electrical excitation through the tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this compare with smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes cardiac fibres as branched and smooth muscle fibres as unbranched.

p006-i17.exam_note: Branching is a major identifying feature of cardiac muscle.

p006-i18.where_on_page: middle left, fourth cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What appearance feature is present in cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle fibres have striations.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are these striations seen?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are seen as repeated bands across the fibres when the tissue is examined microscopically.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does cardiac muscle show striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its contractile proteins are organised into repeating units called sarcomeres, producing a banded appearance.

teacher_understanding.question: What contrast does the page give with smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striations are present in cardiac muscle and absent in smooth muscle.

p006-i18.exam_note: Striated appearance does not imply voluntary control.

p006-i19.where_on_page: middle left, fifth cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page state about cardiac muscle fatigue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that cardiac muscle fibres do not fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: What evidence is supplied on the page for this statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The statement is explicitly listed as a characteristic. The page gives no fatigue experiment or numerical evidence.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cardiac muscle suited to repeated activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells have abundant mitochondria and a rich blood supply that support continuous aerobic energy production. Alternating contraction and relaxation forms part of its normal repeated activity.

teacher_understanding.question: Does fatigue resistance mean the heart can function without an adequate oxygen supply?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Normal performance depends on an adequate supply of oxygen and nutrients; interruption of that supply can impair or damage cardiac muscle.

p006-i19.exam_note: The book gives fatigue resistance for both cardiac and smooth muscle.

p006-i20.where_on_page: middle left, sixth cardiac muscle bullet
p006-i20.content: • Performs contraction and relaxation in wall of heart.

teacher_understanding.question: What activity does cardiac muscle perform?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contracts and relaxes.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page locate this activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It takes place in the wall of the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: How do contraction and relaxation of the heart wall support pumping?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction raises pressure in a heart chamber to help eject blood. Relaxation allows the chamber to fill again for a subsequent contraction.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is relaxation necessary as well as contraction?
teacher_understanding.answer: Repeated pumping requires renewed filling between ejections. A continuously contracted chamber could not repeat its normal filling and pumping cycle.

p006-i20.exam_note: Connects cardiac muscle location to its mechanical function.

p006-i21.where_on_page: middle left, last cardiac muscle bullet
p006-i21.content: • Helps to pump and distribute blood to body.

teacher_understanding.question: What function follows from cardiac muscle activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It helps pump and distribute blood to the body.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cardiac muscle help blood move?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated contraction of the heart wall generates pressure that drives blood out of the heart and into blood vessels.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does pumping matter for the body's tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood flow delivers oxygen and nutrients and carries away carbon dioxide and other wastes, supporting the activity of body cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What can follow if cardiac pumping becomes inadequate?
teacher_understanding.answer: Body tissues may receive too little blood to meet their oxygen and nutrient requirements.

p006-i21.exam_note: A direct muscle-function matching fact with a clear physiological explanation.

p006-i22.where_on_page: middle left, below cardiac muscle bullets

teacher_understanding.question: Which descriptors does the book give as other names for cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It gives 'Striated' and 'Involuntary'.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this combination differ from the smooth muscle combination?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary; smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can cardiac muscle be both striated and involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striated describes the arrangement of contractile structures, while involuntary describes control. A banded fibre does not have to be under conscious control.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cardiac contractions occur without a conscious command for each beat?
teacher_understanding.answer: Specialised pacemaker cells generate rhythmic electrical activity. Autonomic nerves and hormones can modify the rate and strength of the heart's activity.

p006-i22.exam_note: The striated-involuntary combination is a central cardiac muscle identification fact.

p006-i23.where_on_page: middle right, rectangular cardiac muscle illustration
p006-i23.content: A boxed illustration pairs an orange branching network of cardiac muscle on the left with a heart on the right. The tissue drawing contains blue oval nuclei, repeated short pale bands and openings between the connected branches. The heart is coloured red with blue and yellow regions and prominent vessels at its upper end. The two drawings associate cardiac muscle with the heart; no arrows or individual anatomical labels are shown.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the lower illustration show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows a schematic branching cardiac muscle network beside a heart.

teacher_understanding.question: Which drawn features support recognition of cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The branching pattern and repeated bands correspond to the listed features of branching and striations.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the figure connect tissue structure with location?
teacher_understanding.answer: The side-by-side placement links the cardiac muscle schematic to the heart, whose wall is identified in the text as the site of its activity.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the blue nuclei be interpreted in this schematic?
teacher_understanding.answer: They indicate nuclei within the tissue. Since individual cell boundaries are not clearly resolved, the whole network should not be treated as one cell with many nuclei.

p006-i23.exam_note: Supports recognition of cardiac tissue from its branching, banded appearance and organ association.

p006-i24.where_on_page: middle right figure, beneath the branching tissue
p006-i24.content: Cardiac Muscle — the label names the orange branching muscle tissue shown above it.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the printed tissue label in the lower figure?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label reads 'Cardiac Muscle'.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the figure does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the branching orange tissue schematic above the label.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the neighbouring heart illustration reinforce the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It associates the named tissue with the heart, matching the text's statement that this muscle acts in the heart wall.

p006-i24.exam_note: Links the tissue name to its diagram and organ.

p007-i1.type_note: The heading introduces three named tissue types rather than a visual figure alone.
p007-i1.exam_note: Introduces a frequently tested classification of animal tissues.

p007-i2.content: Comparison of Skeletal, Cardiac and Visceral (smooth muscle). Columns: tissue type, Location, Function, Appearance, Control.
p007-i2.type_note: Shared column headings make this a comparison, although BIE proposed figure for the image.

teacher_understanding.question: On which criteria does the table compare the three muscle types?
teacher_understanding.answer: It compares where they occur, what they do, how they appear and whether their control is voluntary or involuntary.

teacher_understanding.question: Which combination distinguishes each type?
teacher_understanding.answer: Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleated and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striated, has one central nucleus as stated here, and is involuntary. Visceral muscle has no striations, one central nucleus and involuntary control.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a student use these criteria to identify an unfamiliar muscle sample?
teacher_understanding.answer: Combine appearance with location and control. Striations alone cannot distinguish skeletal from cardiac muscle, because the table assigns striations to both.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does involuntary control not imply a smooth appearance?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cardiac row combines involuntary control with striations. Appearance and control are separate comparison criteria.

prerequisites: tissue as a group of specialised cells
p007-i2.exam_note: Supports matching, statement-based questions and elimination using appearance, location and control.

p007-i3.content: Tissue-type column: unlabelled | Location | Function | Appearance | Control
p007-i3.type_note: The row supplies the criteria for the tissue comparison.
p007-i3.exam_note: Provides the framework for reading the three tissue rows.

p007-i4.content: Skeletal | Location: skeleton | Function: movement, heat, posture | Appearance: striated, multi-nucleated (eccentric), fibers parallel | Control: voluntary
p007-i4.type_note: This row describes one tissue through the table's shared comparison criteria.

teacher_understanding.question: How does skeletal muscle compare with the other two types?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the voluntary type in this table. Like cardiac muscle it is striated, but it has multiple eccentric nuclei and parallel fibers; smooth muscle lacks striations.

teacher_understanding.question: What location and functions distinguish the skeletal row?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its location is the skeleton, and its functions are movement, heat and posture. The cardiac row instead emphasises pumping blood, while the visceral row lists internal-organ functions.

teacher_understanding.question: What do 'striated', 'multi-nucleated' and 'eccentric' mean here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striated means showing repeated light and dark bands. Multinucleated means that one muscle fiber contains several nuclei. Eccentric means that the nuclei lie away from the centre, near the fiber's periphery.

teacher_understanding.question: How can skeletal muscle support movement and posture?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction develops tension that pulls through attachments to the skeleton. Coordinated contractions move body parts, while sustained activity in selected muscles helps maintain posture.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the table include heat as a muscle function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Muscle activity uses chemical energy, part of which is released as heat. Shivering is a familiar example of muscle contractions helping generate body heat.

p007-i4.exam_note: Remember the linked set: skeleton, voluntary control, striations, multiple peripheral nuclei and parallel fibers.

p007-i5.content: A long cylindrical pink skeletal muscle fiber with repeated transverse bands and several purple nuclei at different positions along its length.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this illustration show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It illustrates the banded, elongated appearance of skeletal muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible features agree with the skeletal-muscle row?
teacher_understanding.answer: Repeated bands correspond to striations, and several purple nuclear profiles correspond to its multinucleated appearance.

teacher_understanding.question: How do striations arise in skeletal muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Regularly arranged contractile filaments produce repeating light and dark regions along the fiber.

p007-i5.exam_note: Useful for recognising skeletal muscle in a diagram.

p007-i6.content: Cardiac | Location: heart | Function: pump blood continuously | Appearance: striated, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary
p007-i6.type_note: This row compares cardiac muscle with the other tissues using the same four criteria.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cardiac muscle share features with both other muscle types?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shares striations with skeletal muscle and involuntary control with visceral muscle. The table gives it one central nucleus, as it does for visceral muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes its location and function?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in the heart and pumps blood continuously, rather than moving the skeleton or carrying out the listed visceral functions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cardiac muscle contraction pump blood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction of the muscular heart wall raises pressure in the chambers and drives blood onward through the circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is involuntary control appropriate to this function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Circulation must continue during sleep and without repeated conscious decisions. Cardiac rhythm is generated within the heart and adjusted by nervous and hormonal influences.

p007-i6.exam_note: Cardiac muscle is the key example showing that striated muscle can be involuntary.

p007-i7.content: Pink striated cardiac muscle fibers branch and connect, with purple nuclei visible within the fibers.

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement is visible in the cardiac-muscle illustration?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibers form a branching, connected arrangement rather than a single straight cylinder.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visual features help identify this as cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The illustration combines branching fibers, striations and nuclei located within the fibers.

teacher_understanding.question: How does connection between cardiac cells support their function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Specialised junctions mechanically link neighbouring cells and permit electrical communication, helping their contractions act together.

p007-i7.exam_note: Branching and striations help distinguish cardiac muscle in identification questions.

p007-i8.content: Visceral (smooth muscle) | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: Peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary
p007-i8.type_note: This row compares smooth muscle with skeletal and cardiac muscle through shared criteria.

teacher_understanding.question: How does visceral muscle compare with the other two types?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is involuntary like cardiac muscle, but lacks the striations found in both cardiac and skeletal muscle. The table gives it one central nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations and functions identify the visceral row?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its locations are the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels. Its functions are peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and erection of hairs.

teacher_understanding.question: What does G.I. tract mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: G.I. means gastrointestinal: the digestive passage through which food and its residues move.

teacher_understanding.question: How does smooth muscle produce peristalsis?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated waves of contraction and relaxation in the wall of the digestive tract propel its contents along.

teacher_understanding.question: How do smooth muscles affect blood pressure and pupil size?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction or relaxation in blood-vessel walls changes vessel diameter and influences resistance to blood flow. Smooth muscles in the iris change the size of the pupil.

teacher_understanding.question: How does smooth muscle erect hairs?
teacher_understanding.answer: Small arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles contract and pull hairs more upright, producing goosebumps. This explains the listed function, although the location column does not separately mention skin.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does 'no striations' not mean that this muscle cannot contract?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle contains contractile proteins, but they lack the regular band-producing arrangement seen in striated muscle.

p007-i8.exam_note: Locations and involuntary non-striated appearance are important for matching and odd-one-out questions.

p007-i9.content: An elongated spindle-shaped smooth muscle cell, tapering at both ends, with a central purple nucleus and no visible transverse striations.

teacher_understanding.question: What shape does the smooth-muscle illustration show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows a spindle-shaped cell: broader in the middle and tapering towards both ends.

teacher_understanding.question: Which features match the appearance stated in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: A single nucleus occupies the central region, and transverse bands are absent.

teacher_understanding.question: How can this drawing be distinguished from the skeletal-muscle drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Use its tapered ends, single central nucleus and unbanded appearance, compared with the cylindrical, banded, multinucleated skeletal fiber.

p007-i9.exam_note: Common visual identification of smooth muscle.

p007-i10.content: Five labelled panels illustrate connective tissues: (a) types of blood cells, showing different white blood corpuscles and platelets; (b) compact bone, showing circular units around Haversian canals and canaliculi; (c) hyaline cartilage, showing chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix; (d) areolar tissue, showing cells among collagen and reticular fibres; (e) adipose tissue, showing adipocytes with large fat droplets and displaced nuclei.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this composite figure illustrate?
teacher_understanding.answer: It illustrates blood cells, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue as examples of connective tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Which panel corresponds to each tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (a) shows blood cells; (b) compact bone; (c) hyaline cartilage; (d) areolar tissue; and (e) adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How can tissues with such different appearances belong to one broad group?
teacher_understanding.answer: Connective tissues have cells associated with an extracellular matrix. The matrix varies greatly: it is fluid in blood, firm in cartilage and mineralised in bone.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should students examine both cells and their surrounding material?
teacher_understanding.answer: The nature and arrangement of the matrix help distinguish connective tissues and explain their different functions, such as transport, support, binding and storage.

p007-i10.exam_note: Connective-tissue examples, identifying features and labelled components support matching questions.

p007-i11.content: Different white blood corpuscles — identifies the illustrated group of white blood cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What group does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the different white blood corpuscles illustrated in the blood-cell panel.

teacher_understanding.question: Which named white blood cells are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte and monocyte.

teacher_understanding.question: How do white blood corpuscles contribute to the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: Different types participate in defence through activities such as engulfing microbes, producing immune responses and releasing substances involved in inflammation.

p007-i11.exam_note: Recognise the named white blood cell types.

p007-i12.where_on_page: blood-cell panel, above the upper cells
p007-i12.content: Cytoplasm — leader line points to the cell material surrounding a white blood cell's nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: What component is labelled Cytoplasm?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label identifies material inside the cell around its nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Which region should be distinguished from the nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: The surrounding cytoplasmic region is distinct from the darker nuclear region.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cytoplasm support cell activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains the medium and cell components in which many metabolic reactions and cellular activities occur.

p007-i12.exam_note: Supports correct interpretation of cellular diagrams.

p007-i13.content: Nucleus — leader line points to the darker internal structure of a white blood corpuscle.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Nucleus label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the darker internal nuclear structure within an illustrated white blood cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Which feature varies visibly among the illustrated white blood cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their nuclei differ in shape, including lobed, rounded and indented forms.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the nucleus contribute to cell function?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains genetic material and helps regulate gene expression and cellular activity.

p007-i13.exam_note: Nuclear shape helps interpret blood-cell illustrations.

p007-i14.content: Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte) — names the illustrated white blood cell with a lobed nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell is identified by this label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies a neutrophil, also labelled polymorphonuclear leucocyte.

teacher_understanding.question: Which nuclear feature is associated with this illustrated cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: The nucleus has a lobed appearance.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should 'polymorphonuclear' not be confused with skeletal muscle's 'multi-nucleated'?
teacher_understanding.answer: A neutrophil has a nucleus divided into connected lobes; a skeletal muscle fiber contains multiple separate nuclei.

teacher_understanding.question: How do neutrophils help defend the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: They can engulf and destroy invading microbes through phagocytosis.

p007-i14.exam_note: Useful for matching leucocyte names and recognising lobed nuclei.

p007-i15.content: Eosinophil — names the upper middle white blood cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Eosinophil label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies one of the illustrated white blood corpuscles.

teacher_understanding.question: Which broader blood-cell group includes eosinophils?
teacher_understanding.answer: The figure places them among the different white blood corpuscles.

teacher_understanding.question: How do eosinophils contribute to defence?
teacher_understanding.answer: They participate in responses to certain parasites and in allergic and inflammatory reactions.

p007-i15.exam_note: Know eosinophil as a white blood cell, distinct from erythrocytes and platelets.

p007-i16.content: Basophil — names the upper-right white blood cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell does this label name?
teacher_understanding.answer: It names a basophil in the blood-cell panel.

teacher_understanding.question: Which group includes basophils in the illustration?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are included among white blood corpuscles.

teacher_understanding.question: How do basophils participate in body responses?
teacher_understanding.answer: They release substances such as histamine that contribute to inflammatory and allergic responses.

p007-i16.exam_note: Useful in classification and blood-cell matching questions.

p007-i17.content: Lymphocyte — names the lower-left white blood cell with a prominent rounded nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell is labelled Lymphocyte?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the lower-left white blood corpuscle in the panel.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible structure occupies much of this cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: A prominent rounded nucleus occupies much of the illustrated cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How do lymphocytes contribute to immunity?
teacher_understanding.answer: Different lymphocyte types have different roles; B lymphocytes can give rise to antibody-secreting plasma cells, while T lymphocytes participate in cell-mediated immune responses.

p007-i17.exam_note: Links blood-cell identification with immune function.

p007-i18.content: Monocyte — names the lower middle white blood cell with an indented nuclear profile.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies a monocyte among the illustrated white blood corpuscles.

teacher_understanding.question: Which nuclear shape helps distinguish its drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its nuclear profile is indented rather than simply round.

teacher_understanding.question: How are monocytes related to macrophages?
teacher_understanding.answer: Monocytes circulate in blood and can enter tissues and develop into macrophages, which engulf particles and microbes.

p007-i18.exam_note: Connects the blood panel with the macrophage labelled in areolar tissue.

p007-i19.content: Platelets — identifies the small clustered elements beside the lower white blood cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Platelets label point to?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the small clustered elements shown beside the white blood cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which illustrated blood elements are much smaller than the neighbouring white blood cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: The platelets are drawn as much smaller elements.

teacher_understanding.question: How do platelets help after a blood vessel is injured?
teacher_understanding.answer: They adhere and aggregate at the damaged site and help initiate processes that form a clot and reduce blood loss.

p007-i19.exam_note: Distinguish platelets and their clotting role from white and red blood cells.

p007-i20.where_on_page: compact-bone panel (b), label above circular units
p007-i20.content: Haversian canal (contains blood vessels and nerve fibres) — points to the central canal of a compact-bone unit.

teacher_understanding.question: What is labelled in the centre of the compact-bone unit?
teacher_understanding.answer: A Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerve fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue panel contains this structure?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in panel (b), compact bone.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are blood vessels important within compact bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone contains living cells that require nutrients and oxygen and must remove metabolic wastes. Vessels in its canals provide routes for exchange.

p007-i20.exam_note: Haversian canals and their contents are characteristic identification facts for compact bone.

p007-i21.content: Canaliculus (contains slender process of bone cell or osteocyte) — identifies a fine channel associated with a bone cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What does a canaliculus contain according to the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains a slender process of a bone cell, or osteocyte.

teacher_understanding.question: Which is the larger vessel-containing structure: a canaliculus or the Haversian canal?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Haversian canal is the central vessel-containing canal; canaliculi are the fine channels associated with osteocyte processes.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these fine channels help cells embedded in hard bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: They accommodate cell processes and support communication and exchange between osteocytes and nearby sources of nutrients.

p007-i21.exam_note: Distinguish canaliculi from the Haversian canal and retain the term osteocyte.

p007-i22.content: Red blood corpuscle — names the small illustrated blood element below the compact-bone region; its exact association within the crowded inset is unclear.

teacher_understanding.question: Which blood element is named by this label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label names a red blood corpuscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Which familiar blood-cell name corresponds to red blood corpuscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Erythrocyte is another name for a red blood corpuscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How do red blood corpuscles contribute to transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their haemoglobin binds oxygen and enables much of the blood's oxygen transport.

p007-i22.exam_note: Distinguish oxygen-carrying red blood corpuscles from defensive leucocytes and platelets.

p007-i23.content: Chondrocyte — points to a cartilage cell embedded in the illustrated cartilage.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell is labelled in the cartilage panel?
teacher_understanding.answer: A chondrocyte, or cartilage cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue panel contains the labelled chondrocyte?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (c), hyaline cartilage.

teacher_understanding.question: How do chondrocytes contribute to cartilage?
teacher_understanding.answer: They produce and maintain the surrounding cartilage matrix.

p007-i23.exam_note: Chondrocyte–cartilage is a standard cell–tissue match.

p007-i24.content: Hyaline matrix — points to the material surrounding the cartilage cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Hyaline matrix label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the surrounding material in which the cartilage cells are embedded.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two labelled components should be distinguished in this panel?
teacher_understanding.answer: The chondrocyte is the cell; the hyaline matrix is the surrounding extracellular material.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cartilage matrix support its function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its hydrated extracellular material and fibres provide resilient support and help resist compression.

p007-i24.exam_note: Supports distinction between connective-tissue cells and matrix.

p007-i25.content: Reticular fibre — points to a fine fibre within the areolar-tissue network.

teacher_understanding.question: What component does this label name?
teacher_understanding.answer: A reticular fibre in the areolar-tissue illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Which connective-tissue panel includes this labelled fibre?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (d), areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do reticular fibres contribute to tissue organisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: They form delicate supporting networks around cells and other tissue components.

p007-i25.exam_note: Recognise a fibre component rather than a cell type.

p007-i26.content: Fibroblast — points to an elongated cell among the connective-tissue fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies a fibroblast in the areolar-tissue panel.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue contains the illustrated fibroblast?
teacher_understanding.answer: The figure places it in areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibroblasts help form connective tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: They produce extracellular matrix components, including fibres and ground substance, and contribute to tissue repair.

p007-i26.exam_note: Fibroblast is an important connective-tissue cell and matrix-producing cell.

p007-i27.content: Macrophage — points to an irregular cell among the tissue fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell does this label name?
teacher_understanding.answer: A macrophage in areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Which illustrated connective tissue contains this macrophage?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (d), areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a macrophage protect and maintain tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It engulfs microbes, foreign particles and cellular debris through phagocytosis.

p007-i27.exam_note: Match macrophages with phagocytosis and connective tissue.

p007-i28.content: Collagen fibre — points to a prominent fibre bundle crossing the areolar-tissue illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: What structure is labelled Collagen fibre?
teacher_understanding.answer: A fibre bundle within the areolar-tissue matrix.

teacher_understanding.question: Which other fibre is explicitly labelled in the same panel?
teacher_understanding.answer: Reticular fibre is also labelled.

teacher_understanding.question: How do collagen fibres contribute to tissue strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their protein bundles resist tensile forces, helping tissue withstand pulling and stretching.

p007-i28.exam_note: Collagen fibres are important structural components of connective tissue.

p007-i29.content: Mast cell — points to a cell among the fibres of areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: A mast cell in the areolar-tissue illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue panel includes the mast cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (d), areolar tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do mast cells participate in tissue responses?
teacher_understanding.answer: They release chemical mediators, including histamine, that contribute to inflammation and allergic responses.

p007-i29.exam_note: Recognise mast cells as connective-tissue cells associated with inflammatory mediators.

p007-i30.content: Plasma cell — points to a rounded cell at the right of the areolar-tissue illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: A plasma cell in the areolar-tissue panel.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labelled item here is a cell rather than the fluid portion of blood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plasma cell names a cell; it should not be confused with blood plasma.

teacher_understanding.question: How do plasma cells contribute to defence?
teacher_understanding.answer: They develop from activated B lymphocytes and secrete antibodies.

p007-i30.exam_note: Distinguish plasma cells from plasma and connect them with antibody production.

p007-i31.content: Fat droplet — points to the large pale internal region of an adipocyte.

teacher_understanding.question: What occupies much of the illustrated fat cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: A large fat droplet occupies much of the adipocyte.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue panel contains the labelled fat droplet?
teacher_understanding.answer: Panel (e), adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a fat droplet relate to adipose-tissue function?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores lipid that serves as an energy reserve. Adipose tissue also contributes to insulation and cushioning.

p007-i31.exam_note: Large stored-fat droplets are an identifying feature of adipose tissue.

p007-i32.content: Nucleus — leader lines point to small dark peripheral structures in the illustrated adipocytes.

teacher_understanding.question: What structures do the Nucleus leader lines identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: They identify the small dark nuclei near the edges of the illustrated fat cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which position characterises the nuclei in this adipose-tissue drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are displaced towards the cell periphery.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the nucleus peripheral in these illustrated adipocytes?
teacher_understanding.answer: The large stored-fat droplet occupies most of the cell and displaces the nucleus and much of the cytoplasm towards the edge.

p007-i32.exam_note: Peripheral nuclei help identify typical white adipose tissue.

p007-i33.content: Adipocyte — identifies a fat-storing cell in the adipose-tissue panel.

teacher_understanding.question: What cell is named Adipocyte?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label names a cell in the adipose-tissue illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labelled components identify its illustrated organisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: A large fat droplet and a peripheral nucleus are labelled in the same panel.

teacher_understanding.question: How is an adipocyte specialised for storage?
teacher_understanding.answer: It accumulates substantial quantities of lipid within its cytoplasm, providing a reserve that can be mobilised when energy is needed.

p007-i33.exam_note: Adipocyte–adipose tissue is a standard cell–tissue association.

p007-i34.content: Fig. 6.10: Types of connective tissues: (a) types of blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue, (e) adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the caption establish about these five panels?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are presented as types of connective tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Which panel letters correspond to cartilage and the two loose connective-tissue examples?
teacher_understanding.answer: Hyaline cartilage is (c), areolar tissue is (d), and adipose tissue is (e).

teacher_understanding.question: How does the caption prevent misidentification of this crowded illustration?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides a direct letter-to-tissue key, so each collection of labels can be associated with the correct tissue.

p007-i34.exam_note: Preserves the complete set of connective-tissue examples on the page.

p007-i35.content: How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?
p007-i35.type_note: The question asks for a transmission mechanism, although the source group was proposed as figure.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the diagram answer its introductory question?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows an electrical signal travelling along an axon towards its tips, which communicate with the next neuron at a synapse.

teacher_understanding.question: When does a neuron pass an impulse onwards?
teacher_understanding.answer: When sufficient stimulation brings its membrane to threshold, an action potential is generated and travels along its axon. At a typical chemical synapse, arrival at the terminal triggers neurotransmitter release.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the signal cross a typical chemical synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neurotransmitter released from the axon terminal diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the receiving cell, changing its activity.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the arrows not be interpreted as showing an axon physically merging with the next cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: At a typical chemical synapse, the two cells remain separated by a small cleft; chemical signalling links their electrical activity.

p007-i35.exam_note: Instructional question on signal direction and neuron-to-neuron communication.

p007-i36.content: Two neurons are arranged from lower left to upper right. An axon of a previous neuron approaches the first neuron's receiving region at a circled synapse. The first neuron has dendrites, a cell body and a nucleus. Its axon extends rightwards and curves upwards; blue arrows labelled electrical signal point along it towards axon tips. The tips approach dendrites of the next neuron at another circled synapse. The next neuron's cell body and nucleus are labelled.

teacher_understanding.question: What relationship does the diagram show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows successive neurons communicating: an incoming axon contacts one neuron, whose own axon carries a signal towards the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labels establish the direction of the illustrated message?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Axon of previous neuron', 'electrical signal', 'axon tips' and 'dendrites of next neuron' establish the progression.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the diagram be traced?
teacher_understanding.answer: Begin at the previous neuron's axon on the left, follow its contact with the first neuron, then follow the first neuron's axon and blue arrows to its tips near the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the diagram use a long axon and branched receiving regions?
teacher_understanding.answer: An axon conducts output away from the cell body, while dendritic branches provide sites for receiving signals from other cells.

p007-i36.exam_note: Supports neuron labelling, direction-of-transmission questions and identification of synapses.

p007-i37.content: axon of previous neuron — points to the incoming process approaching the first neuron from the left.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the incoming process labelled?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the axon of a previous neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which neuron sends the incoming message represented at the left?
teacher_understanding.answer: A previous neuron, whose cell body is outside the main illustrated sequence.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this axon relate to the first displayed neuron?
teacher_understanding.answer: It brings output from the previous neuron to a synaptic contact with the displayed neuron's receiving region.

p007-i37.exam_note: Prevents confusing an incoming axon from another neuron with the receiving neuron's dendrite.

p007-i38.content: synapse — points to the circled contact region between the previous neuron's axon and the first displayed neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the lower-left Synapse label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the contact region where the previous neuron's axon approaches the first neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two successive neurons communicate at this site?
teacher_understanding.answer: The previous neuron and the first fully displayed neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How is communication typically achieved at this contact?
teacher_understanding.answer: At a chemical synapse, the sending axon terminal releases neurotransmitter, which acts on receptors of the receiving cell.

p007-i38.exam_note: Recognise synapse as the communication junction between successive neurons.

p007-i39.where_on_page: neuron diagram, above first cell body
p007-i39.content: neuron cell body — points to the expanded orange central region of the first displayed neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What region does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The expanded cell body of the first displayed neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labelled structure lies inside this cell body?
teacher_understanding.answer: The nucleus lies within it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the cell body support the neuron?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains the nucleus and much of the machinery needed for metabolism and protein synthesis, and participates in integrating incoming signals.

p007-i40.content: nucleus — points to the dark oval within the first neuron's cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the dark oval in the first cell body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the labelled nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Which main neuron region contains it in this diagram?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cell body contains it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the nucleus contribute to neuronal maintenance?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its genetic material directs production of proteins needed for the neuron's structure, metabolism and signalling machinery.

p007-i40.exam_note: Distinguish the nucleus from the entire cell body.

p007-i41.content: dendrites — points to the short branching processes extending from the first neuron's cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: What are the short branches labelled beneath the first neuron?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are dendrites.

teacher_understanding.question: Which illustrated processes differ from the long outgoing axon?
teacher_understanding.answer: The shorter branching dendrites arise around the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: How do dendrites contribute to communication?
teacher_understanding.answer: They receive many incoming signals and conduct resulting electrical changes towards the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is branching useful for this role?
teacher_understanding.answer: Branching increases the surface available for contacts with other neurons.

p007-i41.exam_note: Know the distinction between receiving dendrites and the outgoing axon.

p007-i42.content: axon — points to the long process extending from the first neuron's cell body towards the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Axon label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the long curved process connecting the first neuron's cell-body region to its terminal branches near the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labelled structure carries the illustrated electrical signal?
teacher_understanding.answer: The axon carries the signal shown by the blue arrows.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an electrical impulse travel along an axon?
teacher_understanding.answer: Changes in membrane permeability allow ions to move across successive regions of the membrane, propagating an action potential along the axon.

p007-i42.exam_note: Axon identity and signal direction are central neuron questions.

p007-i43.content: electrical signal — names the blue directional arrows following the axon from the first neuron towards the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What do the blue arrows represent?
teacher_understanding.answer: They represent an electrical signal travelling along the axon.

teacher_understanding.question: Which direction do they show?
teacher_understanding.answer: They point away from the first neuron's cell body and towards its axon tips near the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'electrical signal' be understood biologically?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a travelling change in voltage across the cell membrane produced by controlled movement of ions.

p007-i43.exam_note: Use arrows to establish the illustrated direction of transmission.

p007-i44.where_on_page: neuron diagram, right of central axon termination
p007-i44.content: axon tips — points to the terminal branches of the first neuron's axon near the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Axon tips identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies terminal branches at the end of the first neuron's axon.

teacher_understanding.question: Which neuron's receiving region lies near these tips?
teacher_understanding.answer: The dendrites of the next neuron lie near them.

teacher_understanding.question: How do axon tips pass a message at a typical chemical synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: Arrival of an impulse triggers neurotransmitter release from terminal vesicles, allowing the signal to influence the receiving cell.

p007-i44.exam_note: Identify the sending end at the synaptic junction.

p007-i45.content: synapse — points to the circled junction between the first neuron's axon terminal and the next neuron's receiving process.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the upper Synapse label mark?
teacher_understanding.answer: It marks the junction where the first displayed neuron communicates with the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labelled parts meet at this communication region?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sending neuron's axon-tip region and a receiving process of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this second synapse extend the sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: It allows output from the first displayed neuron to influence the next neuron, continuing communication through successive cells.

p007-i45.exam_note: The two synapse labels illustrate repeated links in a neuronal pathway.

p007-i46.content: neuron cell body — points to the expanded central region of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the upper Neuron cell body label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The expanded central region of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Which repeated features show that this is another neuron?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has a labelled cell body, an internal nucleus and branching processes.

teacher_understanding.question: How can this neuron become the next sender in a pathway?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its incoming signals may bring it to threshold, initiating an impulse in its own axon that carries output onwards.

p007-i46.exam_note: Reinforces that a pathway consists of successive individual neurons.

p007-i47.where_on_page: neuron diagram, right of upper-right cell body
p007-i47.content: nucleus — points to the dark oval within the next neuron's cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the dark structure inside the next neuron's cell body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the labelled nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Which other neuron in the diagram has the same labelled component?
teacher_understanding.answer: The first fully displayed neuron also has a labelled nucleus in its cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the nucleus not be treated as the point through which the impulse must pass?
teacher_understanding.answer: Nerve impulses depend on electrical changes across the cell membrane. The nucleus primarily supports genetic regulation and cellular maintenance.

p007-i47.exam_note: Supports accurate neuron labelling without confusing the nucleus with the signal route.

p007-i48.where_on_page: neuron diagram, far right below upper neuron
p007-i48.content: dendrites of next neuron — points to branching receiving processes of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies dendrites belonging to the next neuron in the illustrated sequence.

teacher_understanding.question: Which sending structure is shown approaching this neuron's receiving region?
teacher_understanding.answer: The axon tips of the preceding displayed neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this label complete the message sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the receiving side after the signal has travelled along the preceding neuron's axon.

p007-i48.exam_note: Pairs the sending axon terminal with the receiving dendritic region.

p007-i49.where_on_page: neuron diagram, blue arrows along the central curved axon
p007-i49.content: Directional arrows run along the axon from the lower-left neuron's cell-body region towards the terminal region beside the upper-right neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: What additional information is supplied by the arrows?
teacher_understanding.answer: They establish the illustrated direction of signal travel along the axon.

teacher_understanding.question: Which neuron sends the signal represented by these arrows?
teacher_understanding.answer: The lower-left neuron sends it towards the upper-right neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the arrows help distinguish axonal conduction from synaptic transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: They show travel along the axon, while the separately circled synapses mark communication between different cells.

p007-i49.exam_note: Arrow direction is essential when tracing a neuronal pathway.

p008-i1.type_note: A pure heading introduces the table.

p008-i2.content: Types of Connective Tissues. Columns: Type of Tissue | Location | Function. Entries: Loose connective tissue; Dense connective tissue; Elastic connective tissue; Specialised connective tissue—(i) Cartilage, (ii) Bone, (iii) Vascular connective tissue (blood); Adipose tissue.
p008-i2.type_note: The visual table compares tissue types by location and function, so comparison is more specific than figure.
prerequisites: A tissue is a group of cells working together
p008-i2.exam_note: Tissue–location–function matching is important for objective questions.

p008-i3.content: Type of Tissue: Loose connective tissue | Location: Deep layers of skin, blood vessels, nerves and body organs. | Function: Support and elasticity.
p008-i3.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How does loose connective tissue compare with dense connective tissue in location and function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue is listed in deep skin layers, blood vessels, nerves and body organs and provides support and elasticity. Dense connective tissue occurs in tendons and ligaments and provides strong, compact binding.

teacher_understanding.question: What structural difference helps explain their different functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue has relatively loosely arranged fibres and more ground substance; dense connective tissue has closely packed fibres suited to resisting pulling forces.

teacher_understanding.question: How can loose connective tissue support organs while permitting movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its fibre network holds neighbouring structures together, while its less compact arrangement allows some movement and deformation.

p008-i3.exam_note: Remember the listed locations and the pairing of support with elasticity.

p008-i4.content: Type of Tissue: Dense connective tissue | Location: Tendons and ligaments | Function: Compactly pack structures to one another and provides great strength.
p008-i4.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do dense and elastic connective tissues compare in their listed roles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dense connective tissue in tendons and ligaments strongly binds structures together. Elastic connective tissue in lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords provides elasticity.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tendon generally connects muscle to bone, while a ligament generally connects bone to bone at a joint.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is dense connective tissue suitable for tendons and ligaments?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its closely packed collagen fibres provide tensile strength, helping these structures withstand forces transmitted by muscles and across joints.

p008-i4.exam_note: Tendons and ligaments are key examples; distinguish their attachments.

p008-i5.content: Type of Tissue: Elastic connective tissue | Location: Lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords. | Function: Provides elasticity
p008-i5.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do elastic and loose connective tissues compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both have elasticity among their listed functions. Elastic connective tissue is listed in lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords; loose connective tissue is listed in deep skin layers, blood vessels, nerves and body organs and also provides support.

teacher_understanding.question: How does elasticity differ from strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Elasticity is the ability to return towards the original shape after stretching. Strength is the ability to withstand force without failing.

teacher_understanding.question: How do elastic fibres help lungs and arteries?
teacher_understanding.answer: They permit stretching and recoil. This helps lung tissue return after expansion and arterial walls respond to pressure changes during the heartbeat.

p008-i5.exam_note: Learn all four locations, including trachea and vocal cords.

p008-i6.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(i) Cartilage | Location: Ends of long bones, tip of nose, parts of larynx and trachea. | Function: Provides flexibility and support.
p008-i6.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How do cartilage and bone compare in this table?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cartilage occurs at long-bone ends, the nose tip and parts of the larynx and trachea, providing flexibility and support. Bone occurs in bones and provides protection, support and muscle attachment.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cartilage more flexible than bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cartilage has a firm but relatively flexible matrix. Bone has a mineralised matrix that makes it much more rigid.

teacher_understanding.question: How is cartilage useful at the ends of long bones?
teacher_understanding.answer: Articular cartilage provides a smooth surface that reduces friction and helps distribute loads as bones move at a joint.

p008-i6.exam_note: Cartilage locations and its flexibility distinguish it from bone.

p008-i7.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(ii) Bone | Location: Bones | Function: Protection and support muscle attachment.
p008-i7.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the listed functions of bone differ from those of blood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone provides protection, support and muscle attachment. Blood transports oxygen and carbon dioxide and contributes to immune response and blood clotting.

teacher_understanding.question: How do bone and cartilage differ as supporting tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone provides relatively rigid support because its matrix is mineralised; cartilage provides more flexible support.

teacher_understanding.question: How does muscle attachment to bone contribute to movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Muscles transmit pulling force to bones through tendons. Bones then act as levers around joints.

p008-i7.exam_note: Associate bone with protection, support and muscle attachment.

p008-i8.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(iii) Vascular connective tissue (blood) | Location: Within blood vessels | Function: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide and immune response blood clotting.
p008-i8.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How does blood compare with bone and cartilage in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: All three appear under specialised connective tissue. Blood is within blood vessels and performs transport, immune response and clotting, whereas bone and cartilage have supporting roles.

teacher_understanding.question: How can blood be connective tissue despite being fluid?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells are suspended in an extracellular matrix called plasma. Connective tissues can have matrices with different physical properties, including a fluid matrix.

teacher_understanding.question: How are blood's listed functions distributed among its components?
teacher_understanding.answer: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; carbon dioxide travels in several forms, especially as bicarbonate in plasma. White blood cells support immune defence, while platelets and clotting proteins help stop bleeding.

prerequisites: Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma
p008-i8.exam_note: Blood is a specialised connective tissue; retain transport, immunity and clotting.

p008-i9.content: Type of Tissue: Adipose tissue | Location: Deep layers of skin, surrounding heart and kidneys and padding around joints. | Function: Support, protection, heat conservation and energy source.
p008-i9.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do adipose and loose connective tissues compare in location and function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are listed in deep skin layers and both provide support. Adipose tissue is also listed around the heart and kidneys and as padding around joints; its additional functions are protection, heat conservation and serving as an energy source.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes adipose tissue from a mainly fibrous supporting tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Adipose tissue contains many fat-storing cells called adipocytes. This stored fat supports its energy-storage and insulation roles.

teacher_understanding.question: How does adipose tissue protect organs, conserve heat and supply energy?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fat deposits cushion structures, reduce heat loss beneath the skin and store lipids that can be broken down when the body needs energy.

p008-i9.exam_note: Remember its locations and all four functions.

p008-i10.content: Plant Tissues branches into Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue branches into Apical meristem, Intercalary meristem and Lateral meristem. Permanent tissue branches into Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue. Simple permanent tissue branches into Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma. Parenchyma branches into Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma. Sclerenchyma branches into Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids. Complex permanent tissue branches into Xylem and Phloem. Connecting lines and downward arrows show classification relationships, not a temporal sequence.
p008-i10.type_note: The diagram presents a hierarchy of tissue categories, so classification is more specific than figure.

teacher_understanding.question: Which are the main divisions and further branches of plant tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant tissues divide into meristematic and permanent tissues. Meristematic tissue includes apical, intercalary and lateral meristems. Permanent tissue includes simple and complex tissues. Simple tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; parenchyma includes aerenchyma and chlorenchyma, and sclerenchyma includes fibers and sclereids.
